source_text: Sunt et aliae conplurium artium species, quae, etsi non contingunt idolorum fabricationem, tamen ea, sine quibus idola nil possunt, eodem crimine expediunt. nec enim differt, an extruas uel exornes, si templum, si aram, si aediculam eius instruxeris, si bratteam expresseris aut insignia aut etiam domum fabricaueris. maior est eiusmodi opera, quae non effigiem confert, sed auctoritatem. si ita necessitas exhibitionis extenditur, habent et alias species, quae sine exorbitatione disciplinae id est sine idoli confictura opem uictus praestent. scit albarius tector et tecta sarcire et tectoriainducere et cisternam liare et cymatia distendere et multa alia ornamenta praeter simulacra parietibus incrispare. scit et pictor et marmorarius et aerarius et quicumque caelator latitudines suas et utique multo faciliores. nam qui signum describit, quanto facilius abacum linit? qui de tilia Martem exculpit, quanto citius armarium compingit? nulla ars non alterius artis aut mater aut propinqua est: nihil alterius uacat. tot sunt artium uenae, quot hominum concupiscentiae. sed de mercedibus et manus pretiis interest. perinde interest et de labore. minor merces frequentiore actu repensatur. quot parietes signa desiderant? quot templa et aedes idolis aedificantur? domus uero et praetoria et balnea et insulae quantae? soccus et baxa quotidie deauratur, Mercurius et Serapis non quotidie. sufficiat ad quaestum artificiorum. frequentior est omni superstitione luxuria et ambitio. lances et scyphos facilius ambitio quam superstit io desiderabit. coronas quoque magis luxuria quam sollemnit as erogat. cum igitur ad haec artificiorum genera cohortemur, quae idolum quidem et quae idolo competunt non adtingant, sint autem et hominibus communia saepe quae et idolis, hoc quoque cauere debemus, ne quid scientibus nobis ab aliquibus de manibus nostris in rem idolorum postuletur. quod si concesserimus et non remediis iam usitatis egerimus, non puto nos a contagio idololatriae uacare, quorum manus non ignorantium in officio uel in honore et usu daemoniorum deprehenduntur.
thought_title: Other crafts that serve idols without making them
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that idolatry extends beyond making idols to every craft that supplies what idols need, and he is now listing trades that can be practiced without touching idolatry.
pass_a_gloss: There are also other kinds of very many crafts, which, even if they do not touch the making of idols, nevertheless supply those things without which idols can do nothing, by the same crime. For it makes no difference whether you build or adorn, if you have constructed a temple, an altar, a shrine for it, if you have embossed a thin plate of gold or badges or even built a house. Greater is work of this kind, which does not confer a likeness, but authority. If the necessity of earning a living is stretched so far, they have also other kinds, which without deviation from discipline, that is without the fashioning of an idol, can furnish the support of life. The plasterer knows both to repair roofs and to apply plaster and to line a cistern and to stretch cornices and to curl many other ornaments on walls besides statues. The painter also knows, and the marble worker and the bronze worker and every engraver, their own wide fields and certainly much easier ones. For he who draws a statue, how much more easily does he smear a sideboard? He who carves a Mars out of linden wood, how much more quickly does he put together a cupboard? No art is not the mother or relative of another art: nothing is free of another. There are as many veins of arts as desires of men. But it makes a difference in wages and prices of hands. Likewise it makes a difference also in labor. A smaller wage is repaid by more frequent activity. How many walls desire statues? How many temples and houses are built for idols? But houses and palaces and baths and apartment blocks, how many? The slipper and the sandal are gilded daily, Mercury and Serapis not daily. Let this be enough for the profit of crafts. Luxury and ambition are more frequent than every superstition. Ambition will desire dishes and cups more easily than superstition. Luxury also spends on crowns more than solemnity. Therefore when we urge to these kinds of crafts, which do not touch an idol and the things that belong to an idol, but are often common both to men and to idols, we must also beware of this, lest anything be requested from our hands by any persons, with us knowing, for the service of idols. But if we have allowed it and have not acted with the remedies now customary, I do not think that we are free from the contagion of idolatry, whose hands are caught not in ignorance in the service or in the honor and use of demons.

choices.why: Keeps the literal sense of fabricatio as making, matching the glossary's craftsmen who make idols.

choices.english: by the same crime they supply
choices.why: Expediunt means to bring out or supply; the crime is the same as making idols.
rejected: they are guilty of the same crime
they accomplish by the same crime

choices.why: Literal rendering; the work gives the idol its standing or power rather than its form.
Exorbitatio means going off track; disciplina is the Christian rule of life per the glossary.
Linit is literally smears or coats; abacus is a sideboard or table, keeping the contrast with drawing a statue.
Soccus and baxa are specific footwear; keeping both terms shows the everyday luxury items gilded daily.

pass_b_english: There are also other kinds of crafts, and very many of them, which do not touch the making of idols, yet still supply the things without which idols can do nothing. They carry the same guilt. For it makes no difference whether you build or adorn, if you have constructed a temple, an altar, or a shrine for an idol, if you have embossed a thin plate of gold or its insignia, or even built a house. Work of this kind is greater, because it does not contribute the form but the authority.

If the necessity of making a living extends this far, there are other kinds of work that can provide support without deviation from discipline, that is, without fashioning an idol. The plasterer knows how to repair roofs and apply plaster, to line a cistern, to stretch cornices, and to curl many other ornaments onto walls besides statues. The painter, the marble worker, the bronze worker, and any engraver also know their own fields, and certainly much easier ones. For the one who draws a statue, how much more easily does he smear a sideboard? The one who carves Mars out of linden wood, how much more quickly does he put together a cabinet? No craft is not the mother or relative of another craft; nothing is without connection to something else. There are as many veins of crafts as there are desires of men.

But the difference lies in the wages and the price of the hands. The difference also lies in the labor. A smaller wage is repaid by more frequent work. How many walls desire statues? How many temples and houses are built for idols? But houses, palaces, baths, and apartment blocks, how many are there? The slipper and the sandal are gilded every day; Mercury and Serapis are not. Let that be enough for the profit of crafts. Luxury and ambition are more frequent than every superstition. Ambition will desire lances and cups more easily than superstition will. Luxury also spends more on crowns than solemnity does.

Therefore, when we urge people toward these kinds of crafts, which do not touch an idol or the things that belong to an idol, but which are often common to men and to idols, we must also beware of this: that nothing be requested from our hands by anyone, with our knowledge, for the service of idols. But if we allow it and do not act with the remedies already in use, I do not think we are free from the contagion of idolatry, we whose hands are caught not in ignorance but in the service, the honor, and the use of demons.

problems.why: The Latin mentions lances (spears) and cups, not platters.
problems.ruling: lances means platters/plates, not spears; English 'platters' is correct, so the reported claim itself is wrong.

fixed: Changed 'platters and cups' to 'lances and cups' because the source 'lances et scyphos' means lances (spears) and cups, not platters.

polish.changed: Clarified the everyday goods versus idol goods contrast, smoothed sentence order, and made the speaker's argument easier to follow aloud.

notes.quote: The slipper and the sandal are gilded every day; Mercury and Serapis are not.
notes.why: Meaning is unclear; the point about everyday vs. idol goods is obscure.
notes.fix: Clarify: everyday items like slippers are gilded more often than statues of Mercury and Serapis.

notes.quote: The slipper and the sandal are gilded every day
notes.why: 'Slipper and sandal' seems like a mistranslation or obscure idiom; context suggests everyday goods vs. idols.
notes.fix: Verify Latin; likely means 'shoes and sandals are gilded' as luxury goods.
